source.title: Towards Neural Scaling Laws for Time Series Foundation Models
source.authors: Qingren Yao; C. Yang; Renhe Jiang; Yuxuan Liang; Ming Jin; Shi-Rui Pan

record.tranche_reason: The study extends power-law scaling analysis to time-series forecasting, but also reports metric- and distribution-dependent scaling and OOD examples whose performance changes abruptly rather than following the expected smooth power-law trend.
record.gate_note: The study trains and evaluates time-series foundation models and reports scaling outcomes. It does not test language-model pretraining loss or downstream language tasks. Prior-work findings cited in the related-work section are not recorded as results. Exact values from scaling curves are generally not stated in the text; rows record the reported qualitative trends. The appendix also reports separate LSF and Monash curves; their individual numeric values are figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study trains encoder-only and decoder-only time-series foundation models across parameters, compute and data. It fits power laws to ID and OOD forecasting NLL/MAPE (plus SMAPE, MASE, CRPS). This is a new modality bearing on V5. Its reports of metric-, distribution- and architecture-dependent exponents, and of non-power-law OOD cases, bear on V7. The results mostly confirm the power-law form, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that encoder-only TSFM NLL scales as a power law with parameters, compute and data on both ID and OOD data. Model size matters more than data. Encoder-only and decoder-only models scale similarly on OOD data, with encoder-only slightly better on ID. Moirai's and Chronos's module designs improve ID performance but reduce OOD scalability. Some zero-shot OOD cases show emergent-like rather than power-law behaviour.
record.recipe_differences: Time-series forecasting models and forecasting NLL/MAPE and related metrics, rather than language models and held-out language-modeling loss; resource factors are investigated separately, and the study includes ID/OOD and architecture comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported patterns vary with metric (NLL versus MAPE and other metrics), target distribution (ID, LSF, Monash, and specific OOD examples), and model architecture/design. The text reports noisy NLL and MAPE during training, attributed as possible effects of the learning-rate scheduler and random-sampling evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: From the ratio of parameter and data exponents, the authors infer that data should grow as D ∝ N^0.8 with model size. They also say compute should prioritise model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint data-to-model allocation for TSFMs is derived from separately fitted single-factor laws, not from a compute-optimal sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models reach lower validation NLL with fewer time points processed (Appendix D.2, Fig. 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models are more sample-efficient (time-series setting).

fits_no_version.finding: Pretrained models need at least about 3M parameters to beat ETS on OOD data meaningfully.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Size threshold for pretraining to beat classical baselines.

record.problems: Most scaling-curve values and uncertainties are not stated numerically in the text; several results are presented in figures. The paper reports noisy NLL and MAPE during training. It focuses on univariate forecasting and says a unified model of parameter, compute, and data allocation is future work.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the selected main-text NLL/MAPE scaling sweeps, appendix SMAPE/MASE/CRPS curves, reported architecture comparisons, ETS comparison, or three emergent-behavior examples. Individual numeric values for plotted curves are not available in the text.

untested.parts: Image or video models, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning and transfer training; multivariate time series.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule and fitting method are not varied. No fitted exponent values are reported in the text apart from derived ratios.
Not tested; no extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
Not tested; no compute-optimal parameter/token split. The authors call a unified model of these factors future work.
Not tested; depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
Not tested for language-model downstream tasks.

missing.what: Chronos-T5 shows power laws in NLL with very small exponents, which the authors attribute to discrete-token prediction. This is a case where the loss barely scales because of output-head design.
Derived numbers from the data law: doubling data gives OOD MAPE about 90% and ID MAPE about 97% of the previous value. These are the only quantitative exponent-derived values in the text.
LSF and Monash OOD curves show a consistent offset and similar slopes across all metrics. Scaling gains follow a fixed proportion across OOD distributions.
A Gaussian-mixture head underperforms a Student-t head, increasingly with model size, and converges unstably. The output-distribution choice affects scaling.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Exact exponents and curve values are figure-only; no uncertainties are reported. The E-* rows split per-size qualitative plots into twelve rows, and a researcher should read them as three dataset-level cases. The data-scaling law uses three points. Training evaluation used random 10% subsets and was noisy.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns time-series forecasting, not language models or held-out language-model pretraining loss.
It does not fit laws on small runs and test their predictions against much larger runs.

It plots lowest loss against compute, but does not establish how the loss-minimising parameter and token counts each grow with compute. The authors say a unified model of the resource relationships remains future work.
The study compares broad TSFM architectures and model designs, but does not hold parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or architecture details across a wide range.

Tests univariate time-series forecasting with encoder-only and decoder-only Transformers, Moirai, and Chronos; it does not test image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer-training regimes beyond its ID/OOD forecasting evaluation.
It evaluates forecasting metrics, but does not test whether downstream-task performance is predictable from language-model scale or pretraining loss.

Reports dependence on metric, data distribution, and architecture, and OOD cases that depart from a smooth power-law trend. It does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, fitting method, or training schedule to compare fitted exponents.

rows.subject: Exponential smoothing (ETS)
rows.operation_detail: Compared forecasting performance of pretrained models with ETS

conditions.value: pretrained models reach at least 3M parameters

rows.value: Pretrained models progressively excel on OOD data as model size increases; the study says at least 3M parameters are needed to surpass ETS at a level justifying pre-training cost
rows.note: The text does not specify which individual metric underlies the threshold statement.
rows.check: Compares pretrained models with a classical ETS baseline to find a size threshold (about 3M parameters). It does not measure the form of scaling, so it should not be linked to V5.

relationships.condition: Encoder-only TSFM sweeps over parameters (~10^3–10^8), compute (six orders) and data (10M–1B points), ID and OOD, all five metrics; decoder-only and Moirai families
relationships.reason: NLL and forecasting metrics fall approximately as power laws in N, C and D for ID and OOD (P-*, C-*, D-*, SMAPE/MASE/CRPS rows, MOIRAI-ID/OOD).
relationships.display_finding: Negative log-likelihood and forecasting metrics decreased approximately as power laws in parameters, compute and data across in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations.

source_check.condition: Encoder-only TSFM sweeps over parameters (~10^3–10^8), compute (six orders) and data (10M–1B points), ID and OOD, all five metrics; decoder-only and Moirai families
source_check.reason: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Appendix D.4 report approximate power-law curves in this modality. The additional architecture comparisons support parameter scaling; they do not establish every architecture-by-metric-by-resource combination.

relationships.condition: Individual zero-shot OOD datasets (us births, nn5 daily, australian electricity); data axis with only three sizes
relationships.reason: On these datasets MAPE changes abruptly between 1M and 10M rather than following a power law (E-US-*, E-NN5-*, E-AE-*). Data-scaling fits rest on three points (D-NLL-ID). Per the text, Chronos-T5's NLL power-law exponents are very small (no row).
relationships.display_finding: MAPE improved abruptly between 1M and 10M parameters; data-scaling fits used three sizes, and Chronos-T5 had very small NLL exponents.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Individual zero-shot OOD datasets (us births, nn5 daily, australian electricity); data axis with only three sizes
source_check.reason: Figure 8 and Appendix D.1 explicitly report departure from smooth power-law behavior on the named individual datasets, with abrupt improvement between 1M and 10M parameters. For this condition group the claimed form is absent. Three data sizes limit fit strength, and small Chronos exponents do not themselves contradict a power-law form.
